cases.headline: Star Health, 2024: a data leak with a customer service bot
cases.subject: Star Health customer data leak
cases.blurb: The company went to court against the distribution channel. That is where the real innovation in this case was, and it was not on the defending side.
cases.description: Policy documents and medical reports belonging to Star Health customers were served on demand by Telegram chatbots, a leak distributed as a self-service product rather than a file.
cases.records: Claims of data relating to around 31 million customers; individual policy documents and medical reports retrievable on request
cases.vector: Not established publicly; the insurer confirmed unauthorised access and disputed the attacker's account of how the data was obtained
cases.actor: An actor operating under the handle "xenZen", who ran Telegram bots distributing the records
cases.cost: Litigation against Telegram and the actor, an interim injunction from the Madras High Court, and a regulatory examination of a listed insurer

cases.headline: National Public Data, 2024: a company you never used, holding everything about you
cases.subject: National Public Data breach
cases.blurb: Nobody in this file signed up for anything. The case that made data brokers a mainstream concern, and showed how meaningless a headline record count can be.
cases.description: A background-check broker most people had never heard of leaked a file advertised at 2.9 billion records, including Social Security numbers, then went bankrupt.
cases.records: advertised as 2.9 billion rows; researchers identified about 134 million unique email addresses
cases.disclosed: Offered for sale April 2024; published broadly in August 2024
cases.vector: Never fully established publicly; a sister site was separately found publishing a plaintext password file
cases.actor: An actor using the handle USDoD advertised the data; it was later posted free
cases.cost: The company filed for bankruptcy protection

cases.headline: AT&T, 2024: who called whom, for nearly every customer
cases.subject: AT&T call records breach
cases.blurb: Metadata is not "less than" content. A complete record of who contacted whom identifies relationships that no message body would reveal.
cases.description: AT&T lost six months of call and text metadata for nearly all its mobile customers. Not what was said, who spoke to whom, how often, and from roughly where.
cases.records: call and text metadata for nearly all mobile customers, about 109 million accounts
cases.vector: A third-party cloud data warehouse account without multi-factor authentication
cases.actor: Part of the campaign tracked as UNC5537; charges followed in late 2024
cases.cost: A proposed $177 million settlement covering both 2024 incidents
exposed: Cell site identifiers for some records

cases.headline: Snowflake, 2024: 165 companies breached without anyone touching Snowflake
cases.subject: Snowflake customer account compromises
cases.blurb: No vulnerability, no intrusion at the platform. Just passwords harvested from employees' machines and accounts that accepted a password alone.
cases.description: Ticketmaster, AT&T, Santander and around 160 others lost data from their own cloud warehouses. The credentials came from infostealer malware, some of it years old.
cases.records: around 165 customer tenants; hundreds of millions of individual records
cases.vector: Credentials stolen by infostealer malware, used against cloud accounts that had no multi-factor authentication
cases.actor: Tracked as UNC5537; two men were charged in the United States in late 2024
cases.cost: Extortion demands against individual victims; regulatory and class action exposure across many companies at once

cases.headline: Change Healthcare, 2024: one login, and American healthcare stopped billing
cases.subject: Change Healthcare ransomware attack
cases.blurb: The largest health data breach in US history, and a month in which pharmacies could not tell patients what their prescriptions cost.
cases.description: A remote access portal without multi-factor authentication let ransomware into the company that processes a third of American medical claims. 190 million people were in the data.
cases.records: about 190 million people
cases.vector: Stolen credentials used on a Citrix remote access portal that had no multi-factor authentication
cases.actor: The ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware group; a second extortion attempt followed from RansomHub
cases.cost: A $22 million ransom paid, and roughly $3 billion in response costs reported by the parent company

cases.headline: The British Library, 2023: the ransom was refused and the catalogue stayed dark
cases.subject: British Library ransomware attack
cases.blurb: The Library then published a frank account of how it had been breached and what it had known. Almost no organisation does that.
cases.description: Rhysida exfiltrated around 600GB and auctioned it. The lasting damage was not the data leaving, it was that thirty years of accumulated systems could not simply be switched back on.
cases.records: Around 600GB exfiltrated, roughly 490,000 files, including employee personal data
cases.vector: Most likely compromised credentials for third-party access on a Terminal Services server provisioned without multi-factor authentication
cases.actor: Rhysida, a ransomware-as-a-service operation
cases.cost: Recovery reported in the region of £6–7 million, met from the Library's own reserves; core services disrupted for the best part of a year

cases.headline: Okta, 2023: the breach arrived through the help desk, inside debugging files
cases.subject: Okta customer support system breach
cases.blurb: A diagnostic artefact nobody classifies as a credential, uploaded voluntarily by customers, holding the keys to their own tenants.
cases.description: Attackers reached Okta's support case system and read HAR files customers had uploaded for troubleshooting. Those files contained live session tokens.
cases.records: Initially reported as 134 customers; later disclosed as affecting the details of essentially all users of the support system, around 18,400
cases.vector: A service account whose credentials had been saved into a personal Google profile on a managed device, used to access the customer support case management system and the HAR files stored in it
cases.actor: Not publicly attributed
cases.cost: Downstream intrusions at multiple security vendors; a revised disclosure a month later; sustained reputational damage to an identity provider
exposed: Session tokens and cookies in uploaded HAR files
Names and email addresses of support system users

cases.headline: 23andMe, 2023: 14,000 accounts opened the door to 6.9 million people
cases.subject: 23andMe credential stuffing breach
cases.blurb: The clearest case of one person's weak password exposing thousands of strangers, and of ancestry data being used to build targeting lists.
cases.description: Attackers logged into 14,000 accounts with recycled passwords. A feature that connects relatives then exposed 6.9 million people who had done nothing wrong.
cases.records: about 6.9 million people, from 14,000 compromised accounts
cases.vector: Credential stuffing with passwords from earlier breaches, amplified by the DNA Relatives feature
cases.actor: Unidentified; data was advertised on a hacking forum
cases.cost: A $30 million settlement, a joint UK and Canadian regulatory finding, and the company's later bankruptcy

cases.headline: MGM Resorts, 2023: a ten-minute phone call to the help desk
cases.subject: MGM Resorts cyberattack
cases.blurb: No exploit, no malware on the way in. A phone call, a name from LinkedIn, and a help desk doing what help desks are measured on: being helpful quickly.
cases.description: Attackers found an MGM employee on LinkedIn, called the IT help desk pretending to be them, and got a password reset. Slot machines and room keys stopped working for ten days.
cases.records: Personal data of customers who transacted with MGM before March 2019
cases.vector: Social engineering of the IT help desk to obtain a credential reset, then abuse of the identity provider
cases.actor: Scattered Spider (UNC3944) working with the ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware operation
cases.cost: MGM reported roughly $100 million in impact for the quarter, plus about $10 million in one-off costs
exposed: A smaller set of Social Security and passport numbers

cases.headline: MOVEit, 2023: one file transfer product, 2,700 organisations
cases.subject: MOVEit Transfer mass exploitation
cases.blurb: The clearest example of supply-chain leverage: attack the software everyone uses to move sensitive files, and you attack everyone at once.
cases.description: A zero-day in a file transfer product let one criminal group steal data from thousands of organisations over a single weekend, most of which had never heard of it.
cases.records: over 2,700 organisations; more than 90 million individuals
cases.vector: A SQL injection zero-day (CVE-2023-34362) in Progress MOVEit Transfer
cases.actor: The Cl0p ransomware group
cases.cost: Estimated in the billions across all victims; a US reward of up to $10 million was offered for information
exposed: Social Security and national ID numbers
Health data, depending on the victim organisation

cases.headline: Latitude Financial, 2023: a licence number from 2005, stolen in 2023
cases.subject: Latitude Financial data breach
cases.blurb: The company refused to pay. The harder question was why it still held identity documents from customers who had finished with it eighteen years earlier.
cases.description: Around 7.9 million driver's licence numbers and 6.1 million older records, some dating to 2005, taken from a lender using credentials stolen from an employee.
cases.records: About 14 million customer records across Australia and New Zealand
cases.vector: Employee login credentials stolen and used to access two service providers holding customer data
cases.actor: Not publicly identified; a ransom was demanded and refused
cases.cost: A ransom refused, remediation and identity document replacement across two countries, and a regulatory investigation

cases.headline: LastPass, 2022: the vaults were stolen, and then attacked offline
cases.subject: LastPass data breach
cases.blurb: Encryption held, mostly. But a stolen vault can be attacked forever, offline, with no rate limit and nobody watching.
cases.description: An engineer's home media server was the way into a password manager's cloud backups. Customer vaults were copied, and attackers have been cracking them ever since.
cases.records: backups of customer vaults, affecting tens of millions of accounts
cases.vector: A compromised developer account, then a vulnerability in third-party software on a senior engineer's home computer
cases.actor: Unidentified; researchers have linked cracked vaults to a series of cryptocurrency thefts
cases.cost: Reputational collapse in the security community; substantial downstream theft from users

cases.headline: AIIMS Delhi, 2022: the hospital went back to paper, and the record stayed thin
cases.subject: AIIMS Delhi ransomware attack
cases.blurb: A case file about the limits of the public record, and why an attack on a hospital in India produced so much less documentation than a comparable one abroad.
cases.description: Ransomware took India's flagship public hospital offline for weeks. What was taken, whether a ransom was demanded, and who was responsible were never established publicly.
cases.records: Reported to involve patient records at national scale; no verified figure was ever published
cases.vector: Not established publicly; ransomware affecting servers hosting the hospital's e-hospital systems
cases.actor: Never publicly attributed with evidence; official statements and press reports did not agree
cases.cost: Outpatient, inpatient, laboratory and billing services on manual processes for roughly two weeks, at a hospital handling thousands of patients a day

cases.headline: Medibank, 2022: the company said no, and the data went up anyway
cases.subject: Medibank data breach
cases.blurb: A contractor's credential with no second factor, 9.7 million customers, and an extortion campaign designed around shame rather than fraud.
cases.description: Medibank refused to pay the ransom. The attackers published 9.7 million customers' health claims data in tranches, organised to cause the most distress.
cases.records: 9.7 million current and former customers; health claims data for about 480,000
cases.vector: Stolen credentials belonging to a third-party IT contractor, with no multi-factor authentication
cases.actor: Actors linked to the REvil ransomware ecosystem; Australia sanctioned Aleksandr Ermakov in 2024
cases.cost: Regulatory proceedings, class actions, and a A$250 million capital requirement imposed by the prudential regulator
exposed: Health claims data including procedures and diagnoses

cases.headline: Optus, 2022: an API with no lock on it, and 9.8 million Australians
cases.subject: Optus data breach
cases.blurb: No password, no token, no rate limit. The breach that rewrote Australian privacy law and put a price on identity documents.
cases.description: An internet-facing Optus API required no authentication at all. Anyone who found it could walk the customer database, including identity document numbers.
cases.records: 9.8 million customers; about 2.1 million with identity document numbers
cases.vector: An internet-facing API endpoint that required no authentication and allowed enumeration of customer records
cases.actor: An extortionist who posted samples, demanded US$1 million, then withdrew the demand
cases.cost: Regulatory proceedings by two Australian regulators, a class action, and the cost of reissuing identity documents nationwide

cases.headline: Uber, 2022: multi-factor authentication held, and then somebody sent a WhatsApp message
cases.subject: Uber 2022 internal systems breach
cases.blurb: Proof that MFA is not a yes-or-no question. The second factor worked exactly as designed and the attacker went through the person holding it.
cases.description: A contractor's password was bought, their phone was buried in approval prompts, and a helpful message finished the job. The real prize was an admin credential sitting in a script.
cases.records: No evidence of access to customer accounts or trip data; internal tools, Slack, cloud consoles and vulnerability reports were reached
cases.vector: Stolen contractor credentials, multi-factor fatigue plus social engineering over WhatsApp, then hardcoded privileged credentials found in an internal PowerShell script
cases.actor: Attributed by Uber to Lapsus$; a UK teenager associated with the group was later convicted over a series of intrusions including this one
cases.cost: No customer data loss established; internal tooling compromised, including access to the company's vulnerability disclosure programme

cases.headline: 0ktapus, 2022: one text message, one hundred and thirty companies
cases.subject: 0ktapus phishing campaign
cases.blurb: The difference between the companies that fell and the one that did not was not training, vigilance or luck. It was the type of second factor they used.
cases.description: A single SMS phishing campaign harvested credentials and one-time codes from employees at more than 130 companies. Cloudflare was targeted with the same messages and lost nothing.
cases.records: ~9,900 accounts and ~5,400 one-time codes captured across 130+ organisations
cases.vector: SMS phishing to employees, directing them to convincing fake single sign-on pages that relayed credentials and one-time codes in real time
cases.actor: A group tracked as 0ktapus / Scatter Swine, overlapping with what later became known as Scattered Spider
cases.cost: Not disclosed; downstream compromises at Twilio, Signal, DoorDash, Mailchimp and others

cases.headline: Twitter, 2022: an API that confirmed which account owned which email
cases.subject: Twitter API data exposure
cases.blurb: The damage was not stolen passwords. It was the link between a real identity and an anonymous account, which cannot be undone.
cases.description: A bug let anyone submit an email address or phone number and be told which Twitter account it belonged to. For pseudonymous users, that is the whole threat model.
cases.records: 5.4 million accounts confirmed; a larger compilation circulated later
cases.vector: An API flaw allowing an email address or phone number to be resolved to an account
cases.actor: Reported responsibly in January 2022; the data was later sold and then published
cases.cost: Regulatory inquiry in Ireland; irreversible deanonymisation for affected users
exposed: The linked account handle and public profile data

cases.headline: T-Mobile, 2021: an exposed router, and 76 million people who were mostly not customers
cases.subject: T-Mobile data breach
cases.blurb: The carrier that has been breached more often than any other, and the year it lost the Social Security numbers of people who were never customers.
cases.description: An internet-exposed router led to a data centre and then to records on tens of millions of people, most of whom had only ever applied for service.
cases.records: over 76 million records, including about 40 million former and prospective customers
cases.vector: An internet-exposed router, then lateral movement into a data centre
cases.actor: John Binns, who described the intrusion to journalists at the time
cases.cost: $350 million class settlement plus a $150 million security spending commitment; a later $31.5 million settlement with the FCC
exposed: Account PINs for some prepaid customers

cases.headline: Kaseya, 2021: the update arrived on schedule and encrypted 1,500 companies
cases.subject: Kaseya VSA supply chain ransomware attack
cases.blurb: The fix was already being written when the attack landed. Responsible disclosure and exploitation were running the same race, and exploitation won by days.
cases.description: REvil exploited zero-days in Kaseya's remote management server to push ransomware down the trusted update channel into roughly 1,500 downstream businesses.
cases.records: Roughly 1,500 downstream businesses, reached through 50–60 managed service providers
cases.vector: Authentication bypass and code injection in internet-facing Kaseya VSA servers, used to distribute a malicious agent update
cases.actor: REvil (Sodinokibi), a ransomware-as-a-service operation
cases.cost: A US$70 million demand for a universal decryptor; hundreds of businesses halted, including around 800 Coop supermarkets in Sweden

cases.headline: Air India, 2021: ten years of passengers, lost by a supplier
cases.subject: Air India data breach
cases.blurb: One supplier, many airlines. Passengers who had never heard of SITA had their passport details taken from its systems.
cases.description: Air India lost 4.5 million passengers' data, including passport details going back a decade, because the company that runs its reservation platform was breached.
cases.records: about 4.5 million passengers
cases.vector: Compromise of SITA Passenger Service System, a shared platform used by many airlines
cases.actor: Not publicly identified
exposed: Some payment card data, without CVV

cases.headline: Colonial Pipeline, 2021: one leaked password, and the fuel stopped
cases.subject: Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack
cases.blurb: Not a breach of personal data, a breach of everyday life. The case that turned ransomware from an IT problem into a national security one.
cases.description: A disused VPN account with no second factor let ransomware into the company that supplies nearly half the US East Coast's fuel. The pipeline stopped for six days.
cases.records: Operational shutdown; a limited number of personal records also taken
cases.vector: A legacy VPN account with no multi-factor authentication, using a password found in a breach dump
cases.actor: The DarkSide ransomware group
cases.cost: A $4.4 million ransom, of which about $2.3 million was later recovered by the FBI
exposed: Personal data of a small number of individuals

cases.headline: Facebook, 2021: 533 million phone numbers that were never "hacked"
cases.subject: Facebook 533 million record scrape
cases.blurb: A feature, not a flaw, until it produced a free file of 533 million phone numbers matched to names. The case that made scraping a regulatory matter.
cases.description: Facebook was right that nobody broke in. Attackers abused a feature working as designed to match hundreds of millions of phone numbers to real profiles.
cases.records: 533 million users across 106 countries
cases.disclosed: Data sold in 2020; published free in April 2021
cases.vector: Abuse of the contact importer feature to match bulk phone numbers to profiles
cases.actor: Unknown; the file was eventually posted publicly at no cost
cases.cost: €265 million fine from Ireland's Data Protection Commission
exposed: Some email addresses and dates of birth

cases.headline: MobiKwik, 2021: the breach that was denied while people searched their own KYC files
cases.subject: MobiKwik alleged data leak
cases.blurb: Users found their own identity documents in a searchable portal while the company was publicly denying that anything had been taken. It has never confirmed a breach.
cases.description: Data said to cover 99 million MobiKwik users was offered for sale with a portal where anyone could look themselves up. The company called the reports baseless. The RBI ordered an audit.
cases.records: Alleged 99 million users and 8.2 TB of data, never confirmed by the company
cases.occurred: Reported from January 2021; the sale portal appeared in March 2021
cases.disclosed: Never formally disclosed by the company
cases.vector: Not established publicly
cases.actor: An unidentified seller advertising the data; no attribution was ever made
cases.cost: The Reserve Bank of India ordered a third-party forensic audit; no public penalty followed
exposed: Alleged KYC documents including Aadhaar and PAN card images

cases.headline: Accellion FTA, 2021: the rehearsal for MOVEit
cases.subject: Accellion File Transfer Appliance breach
cases.blurb: The vendor had been telling customers to migrate for years. The ones who had not were breached through a product that was already scheduled to die.
cases.description: Attackers found zero-day flaws in a twenty-year-old file transfer appliance nearing end of life and used them to rob central banks, regulators and hospitals at once.
cases.records: Dozens of organisations; the Washington State Auditor alone reported 1.6 million individuals
cases.vector: Chained zero-day vulnerabilities in Accellion's File Transfer Appliance, a legacy product approaching end of life
cases.actor: Cl0p, working with the group tracked as FIN11
cases.cost: Accellion settled a consolidated class action for $8.1 million in 2022; victim organisations bore their own costs

cases.headline: SolarWinds, 2020: 18,000 organisations installed the backdoor themselves
cases.subject: SolarWinds supply chain attack
cases.blurb: The update was signed, the checksum matched and the vendor was reputable. Every control that was supposed to catch this passed it through.
cases.description: Attackers compromised SolarWinds' build system and shipped a backdoor inside a signed software update. Around 18,000 customers installed it. Fewer than 100 were the point.
cases.records: ~18,000 organisations downloaded the backdoor
cases.vector: Malicious code inserted into the SolarWinds Orion build pipeline and distributed as a digitally signed update
cases.actor: APT29 / Cozy Bear, attributed by the US government to Russia's SVR foreign intelligence service
cases.cost: Tens of millions in direct costs to SolarWinds; the SEC later sued the company and its security chief

cases.headline: Clearview AI, 2020: three billion faces, scraped and sold
cases.subject: Clearview AI facial recognition database
cases.blurb: Every photo in it was already public. That was the company's entire legal argument, and regulators across four continents rejected it.
cases.description: Clearview AI built a face search engine from three billion images scraped off the public web, sold it to police forces, and then had its client list stolen.
cases.records: Over 3 billion images scraped; later reported by the company as more than 30 billion
cases.vector: Mass automated scraping of public social media and websites, plus a February 2020 breach of the company's own client list
cases.actor: Clearview AI itself; the client list theft was never attributed
cases.cost: Fines and orders from the UK, France, Italy, Greece, Australia and Canada; a US settlement restricting sales to private companies
exposed: Source URLs linking each face to its original profile
Clearview's own client list and search counts

cases.headline: Capital One, 2019: a firewall misconfiguration and 106 million applicants
cases.subject: Capital One data breach
cases.blurb: The breach that changed how cloud metadata works. One misconfigured firewall, one request to an internal address, and fourteen years of applications.
cases.description: A misconfigured web application firewall let an attacker ask the cloud for its own credentials, then read 106 million credit card applications out of storage.
cases.records: about 100 million US and 6 million Canadian applicants
cases.vector: Server-side request forgery through a misconfigured web application firewall, reaching cloud instance metadata
cases.actor: Paige Thompson, a former cloud engineer, convicted in 2022
cases.cost: $80 million regulatory penalty and a $190 million class settlement

cases.headline: First American, 2019: 885 million documents behind a number you could count up
cases.subject: First American Financial document exposure
cases.blurb: The company's own penetration test had found the flaw months earlier. The finding was logged, rated low, and not fixed.
cases.description: Sixteen years of mortgage paperwork, bank details, Social Security numbers, wire receipts, sat behind sequential document IDs in a URL, with no login of any kind.
cases.records: About 885 million documents, the oldest dating to 2003
cases.occurred: Documents were reachable from at least 2003 until May 2019
cases.vector: Insecure direct object reference, changing a document number in the URL returned another customer's file, with no authentication required
cases.actor: No known attacker; the flaw was spotted by a real estate developer and published by a security journalist
cases.cost: A US$1 million penalty from the New York Department of Financial Services in 2023, the first settlement under its cybersecurity regulation, followed by a separate SEC settlement over disclosure controls

cases.headline: Collection #1, 2019: 773 million addresses, and nobody was breached
cases.subject: Collection #1 credential aggregate
cases.blurb: The file that explained credential stuffing to the public. No company was breached to create it, it was thousands of older breaches, merged into one attack tool.
cases.description: Collection #1 was not a hack. It was 87GB of everyone else's hacks, merged and deduplicated into a single file built for one purpose: automated login attempts.
cases.records: 772,904,991 unique email addresses; 21,222,975 unique passwords
cases.vector: Aggregation of thousands of earlier breaches into one deduplicated combination list
cases.actor: Unknown; distributed openly on a cloud storage service and a hacking forum

cases.headline: Marriott and Starwood, 2018: a breach that came with the acquisition
cases.subject: Marriott Starwood guest reservation database breach
cases.blurb: Four years of guest records, five million unencrypted passport numbers, and a compromise that was already running when the company was bought.
cases.description: Marriott bought Starwood in 2016. The reservation database it acquired had already been compromised for two years, and nobody found out until 2018.
cases.records: about 339 million guest records
cases.vector: Long-running compromise of the Starwood reservation system, present before the acquisition
cases.actor: Publicly linked by US officials to Chinese state actors; never charged
cases.cost: £18.4 million fine from the UK Information Commissioner's Office

cases.headline: British Airways, 2018: twenty-two lines of JavaScript
cases.subject: British Airways data breach
cases.blurb: Nothing was stolen from a database. The card numbers were copied out of the browser, one keystroke at a time, before BA ever received them.
cases.description: A small change to a script on the BA payment page sent card details to the attackers as customers typed them. It ran for fifteen days and cost the airline a £20 million fine.
cases.records: About 429,612 customers and staff
cases.vector: Malicious JavaScript injected into the payment page, a Magecart-style client-side skimmer
cases.actor: Magecart, a loose set of card-skimming crews; no individual has been charged
cases.cost: £20 million ICO fine, reduced from a £183.39 million notice of intent, plus a settled group claim

cases.headline: SingHealth, 2018: 1.5 million patients, taken on the way to one of them
cases.subject: SingHealth cyberattack
cases.blurb: Most breaches are opportunistic. This one had a name in mind, and the public inquiry that followed is the most candid document of its kind.
cases.description: An advanced attacker spent months inside Singapore's largest health system, repeatedly and specifically seeking one patient's records. A million and a half others were taken en route.
cases.records: 1.5 million patients' personal particulars; about 160,000 patients' outpatient dispensed-medicine records
cases.occurred: Initial compromise around August 2017; bulk exfiltration 27 June – 4 July 2018
cases.vector: A compromised front-end workstation, then lateral movement to a privileged account and queries against the electronic medical records database
cases.actor: A skilled and well-resourced advanced persistent threat group; the government did not publicly name a state
cases.cost: S$750,000 fine for the health IT agency and S$250,000 for SingHealth; a public Committee of Inquiry and sixteen recommendations

cases.headline: Cambridge Analytica, 2018: the breach that was not a breach
cases.subject: Facebook and Cambridge Analytica data scandal
cases.blurb: About 270,000 people took a personality quiz. The API of the day let the quiz collect their friends too, and the friends were never asked.
cases.description: Data on 87 million Facebook users reached a political consultancy. Nothing was hacked. The platform handed it over through a documented feature working exactly as designed.
cases.records: Up to 87 million Facebook users
cases.vector: Legitimate use of Facebook's Graph API by a third-party app, then onward transfer of the data in breach of platform terms
cases.actor: Aleksandr Kogan's app, data subsequently transferred to SCL Elections and Cambridge Analytica
cases.cost: $5 billion FTC penalty against Facebook, a $100 million SEC settlement, a £500,000 ICO fine, and the closure of Cambridge Analytica
exposed: Some private messages for a small subset

cases.headline: Aadhaar, 2018: what the reported exposures actually showed
cases.subject: Aadhaar data exposure reports
cases.blurb: A disputed case, deliberately included. The exposure was in the ecosystem around the identity system rather than in its central database, which is where large identity systems usually fail.
cases.description: Reports of Aadhaar data being sold and leaked through third-party systems were denied by the authority as breaches of its database. Both positions can be true, and that is the lesson.
cases.records: Disputed; reports covered access to demographic details and third-party systems holding Aadhaar numbers
cases.vector: Reported unauthorised access via intermediaries, and third-party systems exposing Aadhaar numbers through unsecured interfaces
cases.actor: Various; the authority disputed the characterisation of these reports as breaches of its database
exposed: Addresses and other demographic details, as reported by journalists and researchers

cases.headline: Uber, 2016: the breach that was paid to disappear
cases.subject: Uber data breach and cover-up
cases.blurb: The data loss was ordinary. The response, payment, non-disclosure agreements, silence, and eventually a criminal conviction for the security chief, was not.
cases.description: Uber lost 57 million records, paid the attackers $100,000 through its bug bounty programme, called it a research payment, and said nothing for a year.
cases.records: 57 million riders and drivers; 600,000 driver's licence numbers
cases.vector: Credentials found in a private code repository, used to reach cloud storage
cases.actor: Two individuals who later pleaded guilty in the United States
cases.cost: $148 million multistate settlement; the chief security officer criminally convicted

cases.headline: Equifax, 2017: 147 million people, one unpatched web form
cases.subject: Equifax data breach
cases.blurb: A patch released in March. An intrusion in May. Discovery in July, because a certificate on the monitoring appliance had been expired for ten months.
cases.description: The Equifax breach exposed 147.9 million people. A patch had been available for two months, and an expired certificate meant nobody saw the data leaving for 76 days.
cases.records: 147.9 million people
cases.vector: Unpatched Apache Struts flaw (CVE-2017-5638) in a consumer dispute portal
cases.actor: Four members of China's PLA, indicted by the US Department of Justice in 2020
cases.cost: Up to $700 million in settlements; the chief executive, CIO and CSO all left

cases.headline: NotPetya, 2017: the update that cost ten billion dollars
cases.subject: NotPetya cyberattack
cases.blurb: It looked like ransomware and was not. There was no way to pay and no way to recover, the decryption key it offered had never existed.
cases.description: A backdoored update to Ukrainian tax software destroyed the networks of shipping lines, drugmakers and food companies worldwide within hours. Damage is estimated at $10 billion.
cases.records: No data stolen, an estimated $10 billion in destroyed systems
cases.vector: Compromised update server for M.E.Doc, Ukrainian tax accounting software, then automatic spread using EternalBlue and stolen credentials
cases.actor: Russia's GRU (Sandworm), attributed by the UK, US and allies in February 2018; six officers indicted by the US in October 2020
cases.cost: ~$10 billion globally. Maersk ~$300m, Merck ~$870m, FedEx's TNT ~$400m, Mondelez ~$188m

cases.headline: WannaCry, 2017: the patch had been available for two months
cases.subject: WannaCry ransomware outbreak
cases.blurb: Stopped by a researcher who registered a domain name for ten dollars, and a lesson about why hospitals cannot simply patch.
cases.description: A leaked intelligence-agency exploit turned ransomware into a worm that needed nobody to click anything. Microsoft had shipped the fix in March. The NHS lost 19,000 appointments in May.
cases.records: No data stolen; more than 200,000 computers encrypted across around 150 countries
cases.vector: The EternalBlue exploit against Microsoft's SMBv1 file-sharing protocol, leaked publicly the previous month and patched by Microsoft in March 2017
cases.actor: Attributed by the UK and US governments to the Lazarus Group, associated with North Korea
cases.cost: Estimated £92 million to the NHS in England alone; 80 of 236 trusts disrupted and over 19,000 appointments cancelled
exposed: Encrypted files across hospitals, manufacturers and logistics firms

cases.headline: Yahoo, 2013–2014: three billion accounts, and three years of silence
cases.subject: Yahoo data breaches
cases.blurb: Two intrusions, every account Yahoo had ever issued, and a disclosure that arrived three years late and mid-acquisition. Still the largest breach on record.
cases.description: Yahoo lost every account it had, three billion of them, in two separate intrusions, then disclosed them three years later in the middle of selling the company.
cases.records: 3 billion accounts
cases.disclosed: September and December 2016; revised to 3 billion in October 2017
cases.vector: Spear-phishing an employee, then forged authentication cookies
cases.actor: Two FSB officers and two contracted hackers, indicted by the US Department of Justice in 2017
cases.cost: $350 million cut from the Verizon sale price; $35 million SEC penalty; $117.5 million class settlement
exposed: Security questions and answers, some unencrypted

cases.headline: Dropbox, 2012: an employee reused a password, and 68 million accounts followed
cases.subject: Dropbox data breach
cases.blurb: The textbook demonstration that one company's breach becomes another company's breach, carried across by a single reused password.
cases.description: A Dropbox employee used their LinkedIn password on a corporate account. When LinkedIn was breached, so was Dropbox, 68 million credentials, revealed four years later.
cases.records: 68.6 million accounts
cases.disclosed: Confirmed at the time as an email exposure; full scale revealed August 2016
cases.vector: An employee's password, stolen in the LinkedIn breach, reused on a corporate account
cases.actor: Yevgeniy Nikulin, convicted in the United States in 2020
exposed: Password hashes, about half bcrypt, about half salted SHA-1

cases.headline: MySpace, 2016: 360 million accounts from a website nobody used any more
cases.subject: MySpace data breach
cases.blurb: Dead site, live passwords. The largest breach on record at the time, and a lesson in why abandoning an account is not the same as closing it.
cases.description: The MySpace passwords were years old and the site was long abandoned. That is exactly why the breach worked, abandoned accounts still hold passwords people reuse.
cases.records: about 360 million accounts
cases.vector: Never publicly detailed; passwords stored as unsalted SHA-1 of the first ten characters, lowercased
cases.actor: Offered for sale by a seller using the name Peace, the same handle that sold the LinkedIn and Tumblr data

cases.headline: VTech, 2015: six million children in a toy company's database
cases.subject: VTech data breach
cases.blurb: Names, dates of birth, genders and the parents they linked to. For some children, also the photographs and messages they had sent.
cases.description: A breach of a children's tablet maker exposed 6.4 million child profiles, along with chat logs and photographs. The attacker's stated motive was to prove it was possible.
cases.records: Around 4.9 million parent accounts and 6.4 million child profiles
cases.vector: SQL injection against the Learning Lodge app store, with passwords protected only by unsalted MD5 and security answers stored in plain text
cases.actor: An individual who gave the data to a journalist rather than selling it; a related arrest was made in the UK
cases.cost: $650,000 FTC settlement in 2018 over children's privacy violations
exposed: Password hashes and plain-text security answers
Chat logs and photographs from Kid Connect

cases.headline: TalkTalk, 2015: a nineteen-year-old and a webpage nobody owned
cases.subject: TalkTalk data breach
cases.blurb: The vulnerable pages came with a company TalkTalk bought in 2009. Nobody had looked at them since, and the attack that worked was fifteen years old.
cases.description: TalkTalk lost 156,959 customers' data to a SQL injection attack on three webpages it had inherited in an acquisition and forgotten about. Teenagers found them.
cases.records: 156,959 customers, including 15,656 bank account numbers
cases.vector: SQL injection against legacy webpages inherited from the Tiscali UK acquisition
cases.actor: A group of UK teenagers; several were convicted, the eldest sentenced to four years
cases.cost: £400,000 ICO fine, then a record; TalkTalk put the incident's cost at around £42 million and lost 101,000 customers
exposed: Bank account numbers and sort codes

cases.headline: Ashley Madison, 2015: when the data itself was the weapon
cases.subject: Ashley Madison data breach
cases.blurb: Good password hashing, catastrophic everything else. The breach that proved some data is dangerous purely because of what it implies about a person.
cases.description: The Impact Team did not sell the Ashley Madison data. They published it, 32 million people, a paid deletion service that did not delete, and consequences measured in lives.
cases.records: 32 million user records
cases.vector: Never publicly established; the attackers claimed insider-level access
cases.actor: A group calling itself The Impact Team. Never identified.
cases.cost: $1.6 million FTC and state settlement, $11.2 million class settlement, the chief executive's job
exposed: Partial card data and transaction records
bcrypt password hashes, plus a weak legacy token

cases.headline: OPM, 2015: 21.5 million security clearance files, fingerprints included
cases.subject: US Office of Personnel Management data breach
cases.blurb: Not identity theft. Counterintelligence. The SF-86 form exists to record everything that could be used to pressure someone, and all of it was taken.
cases.description: The US government lost the background investigation files of 21.5 million people, every relationship, debt and indiscretion disclosed to get a security clearance.
cases.records: 21.5 million background investigation records, 4.2 million personnel records, 5.6 million fingerprints
cases.vector: Stolen contractor credentials, then malware providing persistent access
cases.actor: Attributed by US officials to actors working for China; never formally charged
cases.cost: $63 million class settlement; the agency's director resigned
exposed: Drug use and arrests disclosed on clearance forms

cases.headline: Anthem, 2015: 78.8 million health records and one query that looked wrong
cases.subject: Anthem data breach
cases.blurb: Found because one employee questioned a query he did not recognise. The largest US health data breach of its time, and the largest HIPAA penalty.
cases.description: A database administrator noticed a query running under his own name that he had not run. Behind it were 78.8 million member records, taken over the course of a year.
cases.records: 78.8 million people
cases.vector: Spear-phishing a subsidiary, then stolen credentials into a data warehouse
cases.actor: Two Chinese nationals indicted by the US Department of Justice in 2019
cases.cost: $115 million class settlement, $16 million HIPAA penalty, $39.5 million to state attorneys general

cases.headline: Sony Pictures, 2014: the breach that destroyed the computers on the way out
cases.subject: Sony Pictures Entertainment hack
cases.blurb: Theft, destruction and publication in one operation, aimed at a company over a film. The first breach treated as a national security incident.
cases.description: Attackers took everything a film studio had, emails, salaries, medical records, unreleased films, then wiped the machines and published the contents week by week.
cases.records: about 47,000 individuals' details, plus the company's internal correspondence
cases.vector: Not fully detailed publicly; the malware included a component that wiped drives
cases.actor: A group calling itself Guardians of Peace; attributed by the FBI to North Korea
cases.cost: Destroyed infrastructure, an $8 million employee settlement, and the resignation of a studio co-chair

cases.headline: JPMorgan Chase, 2014: one server without two-factor authentication
cases.subject: JPMorgan Chase data breach
cases.blurb: The rollout of two-factor authentication across the estate was complete except for one server. The attackers found the exception.
cases.description: A bank spending a quarter of a billion dollars a year on security lost contact data for 83 million households because a single server had been missed in an upgrade.
cases.records: 76 million households and 7 million small businesses
cases.vector: Stolen employee credentials used against a server that had not been upgraded to two-factor authentication
cases.actor: Gery Shalon, Ziv Orenstein and Joshua Samuel Aaron, indicted in 2015; guilty pleas followed in 2020
cases.cost: No customer financial losses reported; the intrusion supported a securities fraud scheme prosecutors valued in the hundreds of millions

cases.headline: Home Depot, 2014: 56 million cards through a supplier's login
cases.subject: Home Depot data breach
cases.blurb: Employees had warned for years that the tills were running outdated protection. The breach ran from April to September before a bank spotted the pattern.
cases.description: Attackers used a third-party vendor's stolen credentials to reach Home Depot's network, then ran custom malware on self-checkout tills for five months.
cases.records: 56 million payment cards and 53 million email addresses
cases.vector: Stolen third-party vendor credentials, privilege escalation, then memory-scraping malware on self-checkout point-of-sale terminals
cases.actor: Never publicly attributed to named individuals
cases.cost: Around $179 million in settlements and costs disclosed across consumer, financial institution and multistate agreements

cases.headline: eBay, 2014: 145 million users and a notice nobody saw
cases.subject: eBay data breach
cases.blurb: No card data was taken, which eBay said often. What was taken was everything needed to impersonate 145 million people convincingly.
cases.description: Attackers used a handful of employees' credentials to reach eBay's user database and sat inside for months. The company then handled the announcement about as badly as it could.
cases.records: 145 million user records
cases.occurred: Late February – early March 2014, discovered in May
cases.vector: Compromised credentials belonging to a small number of eBay employees, used to reach the internal network
cases.actor: Never publicly attributed
cases.cost: No major regulatory fine; a multi-state investigation closed without penalty

cases.headline: Morrisons, 2014: the auditor who published the payroll
cases.subject: Morrisons payroll data leak
cases.blurb: He had legitimate access, a legitimate reason to use it, and a disciplinary record he was angry about. No control in the company was designed to stop that.
cases.description: A senior internal auditor with a grudge copied the payroll file of nearly 100,000 Morrisons staff and posted it online. The case ran to the UK Supreme Court and changed employer liability.
cases.records: 99,998 employees
cases.vector: Abuse of authorised access by a senior internal auditor, exfiltrated on a personal USB drive
cases.actor: Andrew Skelton, a Morrisons employee, convicted in 2015 and sentenced to eight years
cases.cost: Morrisons reported spending more than £2 million on the response; the civil litigation ran for six years

cases.headline: Target, 2013: 40 million cards, and the air-conditioning contractor
cases.subject: Target data breach
cases.blurb: The breach that made "third-party risk" a board-level phrase. The way in was a heating and air-conditioning contractor's password.
cases.description: Attackers entered Target's network through a refrigeration contractor's stolen login, then scraped 40 million card numbers from the tills during the Christmas rush.
cases.records: 40 million payment cards, 70 million customer records
cases.vector: Stolen credentials belonging to a refrigeration contractor, then memory-scraping malware on the tills
cases.actor: Never publicly identified; the malware was a variant of BlackPOS
cases.cost: Around $202 million gross; the chief executive and CIO both resigned

cases.headline: Adobe, 2013: 153 million records and the world's worst crossword
cases.subject: Adobe data breach
cases.blurb: A masterclass in how not to store passwords: one encryption key, no salt, and a plaintext hint column that gave the answers away.
cases.description: Adobe encrypted its passwords instead of hashing them, then stored every password hint in plain text beside them, turning the dump into a puzzle anyone could solve.
cases.records: 153 million records
cases.vector: Intrusion into internal systems; source code taken alongside customer data
cases.actor: Never publicly identified
cases.cost: A $1 million-plus settlement with 15 US states, plus an undisclosed class-action settlement

cases.headline: LinkedIn, 2012: 6.5 million hashes that turned into 165 million accounts
cases.subject: LinkedIn data breach
cases.blurb: Unsalted SHA-1, a forum post asking for help cracking it, and four years later the rest of the database. The breach that compromised other companies.
cases.description: LinkedIn stored passwords as unsalted SHA-1. Six and a half million hashes leaked in 2012; four years later the full 165 million-account file went on sale.
cases.records: 165 million accounts (117 million with passwords)
cases.vector: Never fully detailed publicly; passwords stored as unsalted SHA-1
cases.actor: Yevgeniy Nikulin, convicted in a US federal court in 2020
cases.cost: $1.25 million settlement with premium subscribers; a chain of secondary breaches at other companies

cases.headline: PlayStation Network, 2011: 77 million accounts and 23 days offline
cases.subject: PlayStation Network outage and data breach
cases.blurb: Sony said the passwords were not stored in plain text. It took a week to say what they were stored as, and by then the damage to trust was done.
cases.description: Sony took PlayStation Network down for 23 days after attackers took 77 million account records. The ICO later found the attack could have been prevented.
cases.records: 77 million PSN accounts, plus 24.6 million Sony Online Entertainment accounts
cases.vector: Intrusion into application servers running outdated, unpatched software behind an inadequately protected network boundary
cases.actor: Never definitively attributed; several groups were speculated about at the time and none established
cases.cost: Sony estimated around $171 million; the UK ICO fined it £250,000 in 2013

cases.headline: RockYou, 2009: the 32 million plaintext passwords that became a wordlist
cases.subject: RockYou data breach
cases.blurb: Small breach, enormous legacy. The file that taught everyone what people actually choose as a password, and that still ships with every penetration testing distribution.
cases.description: A widget company stored 32 million passwords in plain text and lost them to a basic SQL injection. The file became the wordlist the whole security industry still uses.
cases.records: 32.6 million accounts
cases.vector: SQL injection against an unpatched web application
cases.actor: A researcher using the handle Tom Daly published the flaw; the dump circulated anonymously
cases.cost: An FTC settlement in 2012 covering both the security failure and children's privacy violations

cases.headline: Heartland, 2008: 130 million cards from a company that had just passed its audit
cases.subject: Heartland Payment Systems data breach
cases.blurb: Compliant and breached. The case that separated "passed the audit" from "is actually secure", permanently.
cases.description: Heartland was certified compliant with the card industry security standard. A SQL injection flaw let attackers plant a sniffer on the network that processed 100 million transactions a month.
cases.records: about 130 million card numbers
cases.vector: SQL injection into a corporate web application, then lateral movement and a packet sniffer on the payment network
cases.actor: Albert Gonzalez and associates
cases.cost: Around $145 million in settlements and costs

cases.headline: TJX, 2007: the wireless network in the car park
cases.subject: TJX Companies data breach
cases.blurb: The first mega-breach of the card era. Weak wireless encryption, eighteen months of undetected access, and the reason PCI DSS grew teeth.
cases.description: Attackers sat outside a Marshalls store, broke the shop's weak wireless encryption, and worked inwards until they reached the card processing systems.
cases.records: 45.7 million cards confirmed; court filings suggested up to 94 million
cases.vector: Weak WEP wireless encryption at a store, then lateral movement to card processing systems
cases.actor: Albert Gonzalez and associates; Gonzalez was sentenced to 20 years in 2010
cases.cost: Reported at around $256 million by the company
exposed: Some driver's licence numbers and names
